passages.t: The tradition of the elders and the command of God
passages.happening:
Some Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem with a question. “Why do Your disciples break the tradition of the elders? They do not wash their hands before they eat” (verse 2).

Jesus answers with a question of his own: “And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?” (verse 3). God said to honour your father and mother. But they teach that a man can declare his money a gift devoted to God, and then he need not use it to help his parents. “Thus you nullify the word of God for the sake of your tradition” (verse 6). Then he quotes Isaiah about people who honour God with their lips while their hearts are far away.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells the same dispute (Mark 7:1-13), and the note there explains it. The washing was not about germs. It was about being ritually clean, fit to come near God. The law told priests to wash before serving at the altar (Exodus 30:19-21). The Pharisees, a movement devoted to keeping the law with great care, wanted ordinary people at ordinary meals to live with the holiness of priests. That was a serious aim, not a silly one.

The ‘tradition of the elders’ was the body of teaching the Pharisees had built up to apply the law to daily life. The Jewish historian Josephus says the Pharisees passed on to the people many rules handed down from earlier generations that were not written in the law of Moses, and that the Sadducees, the party of the leading priests, rejected them (Antiquities 13.297). Much of this teaching was later written down in the Mishnah, a book of Jewish law put together around AD 200.

Mark stops to explain the washing for readers who were not Jews (Mark 7:3-4). Matthew explains nothing. His readers knew the custom already.

The gift ‘devoted to God’ is what Mark calls Corban, a Hebrew word for an offering. The note on Mark 7 tells how it worked. Later Jewish teachers agreed with Jesus here: the Mishnah allows such a vow to be undone when it concerns a man's own parents (Mishnah Nedarim 9:1). This is an argument among Jews about how to keep God's law, and on this point both sides came to stand in the same place.

‘Hypocrites’ (verse 7) is a Greek word that first meant a stage actor, someone who speaks a part behind a mask. Jesus uses it for worship that is a performance.
passages.ot:
Jesus quotes two of Moses' commands. “Honor your father and mother” (Exodus 20:12), and “Anyone who curses his father or mother must surely be put to death” (Exodus 21:17). Honouring parents meant caring for them in their old age. It was a command of God, not a custom.

The law also took vows seriously: a man who makes a vow “must not break his word” (Numbers 30:2). So the Pharisees' side was not empty. One command seemed to stand against another. Jesus says the plain duty to parents comes first, and that a vow cannot be used as a door out of it.

Then he quotes Isaiah. In the Berean Standard Bible, Isaiah reads: “These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me” (Isaiah 29:13). The prophet spoke those words to Israel in his own day. Jesus says they fit this case too.
passages.hard:
Is Jesus against all tradition? No. The note on Mark 7 says it plainly. ‘Tradition’ means something handed on, and Paul uses the same word for the teaching he passed on to the churches (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Christians still differ on how much weight church tradition should carry. Some give it great authority alongside Scripture. Others hold that Scripture alone is the final judge of every tradition. What Jesus condemns here is narrower and clear to all sides: any rule that lets a person dodge what God plainly commands.

Are the Pharisees simply villains? Matthew's words about them are sharp, and Christians have often turned them into a picture of all Jews or all Pharisees. That is a misreading. Jesus is speaking to particular men in a particular argument. Paul was a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). Gamaliel, a Pharisee, was “honored by all the people” (Acts 5:34). And the danger Jesus names is a danger for every religious person, Christians first of all.
passages.asks: The vow looked like devotion and worked as an escape. Ask whether any of your religious habits do the same: church work that excuses neglect at home, or giving that makes you feel free of harder duties. Ask who in your family is owed care that you have quietly set aside.

passages.happening:
Jesus calls the crowd and says, “Listen and understand. A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it” (verses 10-11). To ‘defile’ is to make unclean, unfit to come near God.

The disciples tell him the Pharisees were offended. Jesus answers that every plant his Father did not plant will be pulled up, and he calls the Pharisees blind guides: “If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit” (verse 14).

Peter asks him to explain. Jesus says that food goes into the stomach and passes out of the body. But what comes out of the mouth comes from the heart: “evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander” (verse 19). “These are what defile a man, but eating with unwashed hands does not defile him” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
In the Bible the heart is not mainly the place of feelings. It is the centre of the person, where thinking, choosing and wanting begin. Jesus had already said, “out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks” (12:34).

Here Matthew does something different from Mark, and it should be noted fairly. In Mark, the passage includes a short comment: “(Thus all foods are clean.)” (Mark 7:19). Matthew does not have that line. He ends where the argument began, with handwashing: “eating with unwashed hands does not defile him” (verse 20).

Readers explain this in more than one way. Some think Matthew, writing for Jewish believers who still kept the food laws, kept the point narrow on purpose: the question was handwashing, and that is what Jesus settled. Others think the wider meaning is still there in Matthew's own words, since “whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach” (verse 17), and that Matthew simply did not need to spell it out. Either way, by the time the Gospels were written the church had come to see that Christians were free to eat all foods (Acts 10:15; Romans 14:14).

‘Blind guides’ was a pointed phrase. Paul describes a Jewish teacher who is sure that he is “a guide for the blind” (Romans 2:19). Jesus says these guides cannot see for themselves.
passages.ot:
The prophets had already said that the real problem lies in the heart. “The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure” (Jeremiah 17:9). David prayed, “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10). And God promised through Ezekiel, “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).

The picture of a plant his Father planted is from the prophets too. Isaiah calls God's restored people “the branch of My planting, the work of My hands” (Isaiah 60:21). Jesus says that what God did not plant will not last.
passages.hard:
“Disregard them!” (verse 14) sounds dismissive. But Jesus does not tell his disciples to despise the Pharisees, still less to harm them. He tells them not to fear their offence or follow their lead. The judgment, pulling up what God did not plant, belongs to God.

The list in verse 19 is uncomfortable for everyone. It does not describe some other kind of person. It describes what grows in every human heart, the reader's included. That is why no washing can reach it. Only God can make a heart clean.
passages.asks: It is easier to worry about what is out there, the wrong places and the wrong people, than to look at what is in here. Read the list in verse 19 slowly. Ask which of these grows in your own heart, and bring that to God instead of only guarding the doors.

passages.happening:
Jesus goes north to the district of Tyre and Sidon, outside Israel. A Canaanite woman from that region comes to him, crying out, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me! My daughter is miserably possessed by a demon” (verse 22).

Jesus does not answer her a word. The disciples urge him, “Send her away, for she keeps crying out after us” (verse 23). He says, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (verse 24).

She comes and kneels before him. “Lord, help me!” (verse 25). He answers, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs” (verse 26). She replies, “Yes, Lord,” and then, “even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master’s table” (verse 27).

Jesus answers, “O woman,” and then, “your faith is great! Let it be done for you as you desire” (verse 28). Her daughter is healed from that very hour.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story too (Mark 7:24-30), and the note there gives the setting. Tyre and Sidon were old port cities on the coast north of Galilee. Jews and the people of these cities lived close together, and not always as friends.

Mark calls her “a Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin” (Mark 7:26). Matthew calls her a Canaanite. That was the old name for the peoples who lived in the land before Israel, the nations Israel was told to drive out (Deuteronomy 7:1). A Jewish hearer would feel the weight of it: of all people, a Canaanite.

And yet this Canaanite speaks like a believer in Israel's God. She calls Jesus ‘Lord’ and ‘Son of David’, the royal title of Israel's Messiah, the same words blind men in Israel used (9:27). She asks for mercy. She kneels.

Matthew's version is harder than Mark's. Only Matthew tells of Jesus' silence, the disciples' wish to be rid of her, and the words “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” And Matthew does not have Mark's word ‘first’ (“First let the children have their fill,” Mark 7:27), which in Mark leaves a door open.

In the Bible, dogs were mostly wild animals of the street, and ‘dog’ could be an insult. But the word Jesus uses here is a diminutive, a ‘little dog’ or house dog, the kind that lives indoors under the table. The woman takes hold of that picture. House dogs are inside, and they eat from the same meal. She does not ask for the children's place. She asks for a crumb, and she trusts that a crumb from him is enough.

Jesus praises great faith in two people in Matthew, and both are Gentiles: the Roman centurion (8:10) and this woman. Both ask for someone else, a servant and a daughter, and both are healed at a distance, “at that very hour” (8:13).
passages.ot:
God told Abraham that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). Israel was chosen first, but never only for itself. Paul later names the same order Jesus keeps here: the good news is “first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).

And the region of Sidon had seen this before. In a time of famine God sent Elijah to a widow there: “Get up and go to Zarephath of Sidon, and stay there” (1 Kings 17:9). She fed the prophet, and he raised her son to life (1 Kings 17:17-24). Long before, a Canaanite woman, Rahab, had confessed Israel's God (Joshua 2:11), and Matthew put her in Jesus' own family tree (1:5). Outsiders who trust Israel's God run all through Israel's story.
passages.hard:
Many readers find these the hardest words Jesus speaks to a Gentile in the Gospels. He is silent, he says he was sent only to Israel, and he uses a saying about dogs. Christians have read the scene in several ways, and each reading has serious defenders.

A test of faith. Many teachers of the early church read the silence and the hard words as a way of drawing out her faith so that it could be seen and praised. John Chrysostom, in his sermons on Matthew, said Jesus held back so that her faith would be shown. Augustine praised her humility: called a dog, she did not deny it, and so received what she asked. On this reading Jesus knew from the start what he would do.

A statement of the order of his mission. In Matthew, Jesus' work before the cross was truly directed to Israel. He sent the Twelve only “to the lost sheep of Israel” (10:6), and only after the resurrection does he send them to “all nations” (28:19). On this reading the saying states an order in God's plan, not a verdict on her worth, and her faith runs ahead of that order to what was coming.

A real exchange in which she presses him. Some read the scene as a true conversation in which the woman argues and Jesus is moved by her reply. Others answer that nothing in Matthew shows him changing his mind; he grants her request because of her faith. Both agree that she presses him and that he honours it.

The little dogs. Some stress that Jesus' word is the diminutive, the house dog under the family table, which leaves room for her answer. Others think the diminutive softens little, especially in Matthew, where there is no ‘first’. These notes do not settle the question.

What is not in dispute is the end. She is not sent away. She gets all she asked for. And she leaves with some of the highest praise Jesus gives anyone in this Gospel: her faith is great. Nothing here gives any reader leave to look down on any people. The Canaanite is the hero of the story.
passages.asks:
She heard silence, then a no, then a hard word, and she kept coming. She did not demand, and she did not give up. She held on to what she knew of his goodness. Ask how you pray when God seems silent. Do you walk away, or do you keep coming?

The church has made her words its own. In 1548 Thomas Cranmer wrote a prayer for the English communion service in which believers say that they are ‘not worthy so much as to gather up the crumbs’ under the Lord's table, and come anyway, trusting his mercy. Ask what it would mean to come to God like that: with nothing to claim, and everything to hope for.

passages.happening: Jesus goes along the Sea of Galilee, up a mountain, and sits down. Large crowds come, bringing the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute and many others. They lay them at his feet, and he heals them. The crowd is amazed to see the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking and the blind seeing. “And they glorified the God of Israel” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Only Matthew tells this scene in this way. Mark has one deaf man healed in private at this point (Mark 7:31-37). Matthew shows a whole mountainside of people.

Who were these crowds? The phrase ‘they glorified the God of Israel’ has made many readers think they were Gentiles, praising the God of a people not their own. Mark places Jesus in the Decapolis, the region of Greek cities east of the lake, at this time (Mark 7:31). Others note that Matthew names no Gentile region and think the crowd was Jewish, praising their own God. Both readings are held.

Jesus sits on a mountain, as he did to teach in chapter 5. In Matthew, mountains are places where God's purposes come into view.
passages.ot:
Isaiah promised a day when “the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy” (Isaiah 35:5-6). Matthew's list in verse 31 reads like that promise coming true.

Isaiah also pictured a mountain where God would gather the nations: “On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples” (Isaiah 25:6). On this mountain, healing is followed by a meal.
passages.asks: The people laid their sick ‘at His feet’. Many of them could not come on their own. Someone carried them. Ask who in your life needs carrying to Jesus, in prayer or in practical help, and whether you could be one of the carriers.

passages.happening:
Jesus calls his disciples and says, “I have compassion for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat” (verse 32). He does not want to send them away hungry, or they may faint on the road.

The disciples ask where they could find enough bread in so desolate a place. “How many loaves do you have?” Jesus asks. “Seven,” they reply, “and a few small fish” (verse 34). He has the crowd sit on the ground, gives thanks, breaks the bread and the fish, and gives them to the disciples to hand out. All eat and are satisfied. Seven baskets of pieces are left over. Four thousand men are fed, “in addition to women and children” (verse 38). Then Jesus gets into the boat and goes to the region of Magadan.
passages.hearers:
This is the second feeding in Matthew, as in Mark (Mark 8:1-10), and the note on Mark 8 tells more. The baskets here are a different word from the first feeding: big hampers, the same word used in Acts for the basket in which Paul was let down over the wall of Damascus (Acts 9:25).

As in chapter 14, only Matthew adds “in addition to women and children.” The real crowd was larger than four thousand.

If the crowd on the mountain was largely Gentile, as many think, the order of the chapter is striking. A Canaanite mother asked for crumbs. A few verses later a great crowd eats until it is full, with baskets left over.

No one today knows where Magadan was. Mark names Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10), also unknown, and later copyists sometimes changed both names to Magdala, a known town on the lake.
passages.ot: A crowd fed with bread in a lonely place would remind any Jewish hearer of the manna God gave in the desert (Exodus 16:35). Many readers also hear Isaiah's mountain banquet “for all the peoples” (Isaiah 25:6) behind this meal on a mountain, given after the healing of the lame and the blind.
passages.hard: Is this the same story as chapter 14, told twice? Some scholars think so, and point out how alike the two accounts are. Others note the differences: the numbers of people, loaves and baskets, the setting, and the words. Matthew treats them as two events, because Jesus later asks the disciples to remember both (16:9-10). Whatever view is taken, Matthew wants the two meals read side by side.
passages.asks: Jesus noticed that the crowd had been with him three days and had nothing left. He cared about their walk home. Ask whose ordinary needs you are overlooking because you are busy with what feels more spiritual. And ask what past help from God you have forgotten in your present need.
